text: Average and instantaneous acceleration. Average acceleration. The average acceleration is the rate of change for the velocity v. Average acceleration equals delta v over delta t. Equals v final minus v naught divided by t final minus t naught, where t is time. The SI units for acceleration are meters per second squared, or meters per second per second. This means how much the velocity has changed every second, where the velocity can change in either magnitude or direction due to it being a vector. For example, a runner traveling at 10 kilometers per hour due east slows to a stop, reverses direction, and continues to run 10 kilometers per hour due west. Before turning around, the runner had one average acceleration, then a different average acceleration afterwards. This is shown mathematically as, before the turnaround, the average acceleration equals negative v naught divided by delta t sub m minus t naught, which equals negative 10 divided by delta t sub 1. After the turnaround, the average acceleration equals v final divided by t final minus t sub m. Which equals 10 divided by delta t sub 2. The magnitude of the velocity is the same in both directions, however, the direction is different. Acceleration is a vector in the same direction as the change in velocity delta v. Acceleration is a change in speed or direction or both. Note, although acceleration is in the direction of the change in velocity, it is not always in the direction of motion. When an object slows down, its acceleration is opposite to the direction of its motion. The term deceleration can cause confusion because it is not a vector and it does not point to a specific direction with respect to a specific direction. We can say the runner was decelerating before coming to a stop and accelerating afterward, but we shouldn't include the coordinate system unit vector i hat or negative i hat in our analysis. Otherwise, the runner always has a negative acceleration in contrast to our intuition. Instead of using the term deceleration, we describe the motion more accurately with a positive or negative acceleration relative to the coordinate system. If an object has a velocity in the positive direction with respect to the origin and it acquires a constant negative acceleration, the object eventually comes to rest and reverses direction, i.e. our runner in delta t sub 1. Eventually, the object passes through the origin going in the opposite direction, i.e. our runner in delta t sub 2. Checkpoint. Pause and check your understanding. An object has v equals positive 8 meters per second and a equals negative 2 meters per second squared. Is it moving in the positive or negative direction? Is it speeding up or slowing down? The sign of acceleration tells us the direction of the delta velocity, not whether the object is speeding up or slowing down. To decide whether the speed is increasing or decreasing, we compare the signs of velocity and acceleration. If v and a have the same sign, the object speeds up. If v and a have opposite signs, the object slows down. The full sign reasoning table is available on the course web page. Example problem. Racehorse leaves the gate. The problem. A racehorse coming out of the gate accelerates from rest to a velocity of 15.0 meters per second due west in 1.80 seconds. What is its average acceleration? The model. The horse moves in one dimension along an east-west line. We choose east as the positive direction and west as the negative direction. Since the horse starts from rest and ends with a westward velocity, the change in velocity is directed west, so the average acceleration should be negative in this coordinate system. The math. The average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the elapsed time, which is given by average acceleration equals delta v over delta t equals v final minus v naught divided by delta t. The horse starts from rest and west is the negative direction, so the initial and final velocities are v naught equals 0 and v final equals negative 15.0 meters per second. The change in velocity is therefore delta v equals v final minus v naught equals negative 15.0 meters per second minus 0 equals negative 15.0 meters per second. Dividing this change in velocity by the elapsed time gives the average acceleration as average acceleration equals negative 15.0 meters per second over 1.80 seconds equals negative 8.33 meters per second squared. The conclusion. The horse's average acceleration is negative 8.33 meters per second squared. The negative sign means the acceleration points west, which is consistent with the horse increasing its speed westward from rest. Instantaneous acceleration. Acceleration at a time t is found using the same process discussed for instantaneous velocity. We calculate the average acceleration between two points in time delta t and let delta t approach is 0. The result is the derivative of the velocity function v of t and is expressed as a of t equals the limit as delta t approaches 0 of v of t plus delta t minus v of t all divided by delta t. This equals d v of t over d t. We can show that the instantaneous acceleration at t0 is the slope of the tangent line to the velocity graph at time t0. The average acceleration approaches the instantaneous acceleration as delta t approaches 0. Checkpoint. Pause and check your understanding. On a velocity versus time graph, what does a horizontal tangent line mean about the acceleration at that instant? In the first graph, the velocity has a maximum when its slope is 0, which corresponds to a 0 of the acceleration function. In the second graph, there is a minimum velocity when the acceleration is 0. The zeros of the acceleration function give either the minimum or maximum velocity. Calculus note. Derivatives, extrema and evolution. Finding extrema by setting the derivative to 0. One of the most powerful and general uses of calculus is identifying where a quantity reaches a maximum or minimum. Given a function f of x, extrema occur at critical points, which satisfy df over dx equals 0, or where the derivative is undefined. This works because the derivative represents the rate of change of the function. At a maximum or minimum, the function momentarily stops increasing or decreasing, so its slope is 0. In kinematics, setting v of t equals dx over dt equals 0 finds when an object momentarily stops or turns around. In optimization, setting dE over dx equals 0 finds stable equilibrium configurations. In thermodynamics, extrema of entropy or energy determine equilibrium states. This method applies to any differentiable function, not just position or velocity. Using derivatives to evolve a system. Derivatives do more than identify special points. They describe how systems change in time. Many physical laws are written as differential equations, which specify how a quantity evolves. dy over dt equals f of y comma t. Here, the derivative tells us how the system changes at each instant. Solving the differential equation allows us to predict the system's future behavior. Examples. Newton's second law, mdv over dt equals f of x comma v comma t, determines how velocity evolves from forces. Radioactive decay, dN over dt equals negative lambda n, describes how a quantity decreases over time. Population growth, electrical circuits, orbital motion, and climate models are all governed by differential equations. Big picture. Setting derivatives equal to 0 finds where something stops changing, extrema, turning points, equilibrium. Using derivatives in equations tells us how something changes, motion, growth, decay, evolution. Together, these ideas form the mathematical backbone of physics, engineering, and applied sciences. The acceleration function is found by differentiating the velocity function with respect to time, which gives a of t equals dv over dt, which equals the derivative with respect to time of 20 meters per second squared times t minus t minus 5 meters per second cubed times t squared equals 20 meters per second squared minus 10 meters per second cubed times t. Part b. The instantaneous velocity values are found by evaluating the velocity function at each requested time, which gives v of 1 second equals 20 meters per second squared times 1 second minus 5 meters per second cubed times the quantity 1 second squared, which equals 15 meters per second. V of 2 seconds equals 20 meters per second squared times 2 seconds minus 5 meters per second cubed times the quantity 2 second squared, which equals 20 meters per second. V of 3 seconds equals 20 meters per second squared times 3 seconds minus 5 meters per second cubed times the quantity 3 second squared, which equals 15 meters per second. V of 5 seconds equals 20 meters per second squared times 5 seconds minus 5 meters per second cubed times the quantity 5 seconds squared, which equals negative 25 meters per second. Part c. At t equals three seconds, the velocity is positive, but the acceleration is negative, so the particle is slowing down.
